nodes.label: BCS Syllable-Switching Slang (Sarajevo/Zagreb word-scrambling wordplay)
nodes.rationale: The single most important content finding in this language's whole corpus so far: a genuine, historically attested colloquial word-game (vozdra<zdravo, žemka<kažem, đido<dođi, žibje<bježi historically Sarajevo; lima<mali, cobra<braco, Šomi<Mišo, Njofra<Franjo an older layer once widespread in 1960s Zagreb) that reorders a word's syllables, mechanically comparable to English pig-Latin-style play. The footnote explicitly distinguishes this from Belgrade's own extensive but non-syllable-switching slang system. This mechanism now has a second, independent cross-book confirmation: two separate taboo-avoidance-naming findings noted in the Serbian Folk Tales book (established/084, established/088 in that corpus) — both concern deliberate, rule-governed distortion/avoidance of a word's normal surface form for social/protective effect, the same underlying move (systematic phonological displacement of an ordinary word for in-group/protective purposes) as this syllable-switching slang. No specific cross-chunk edge is asserted here per this project's own confirmed lesson from a prior rebuild (fabricated cross-chunk edge IDs are not reliable) — this is flagged in the node description only, for a human or a later same-chunk merge pass to connect explicitly once both chunks' real node IDs are known.

nodes.label: Ekavian vs. Ijekavian Reflex Contrast
nodes.rationale: Systematic jat-reflex correspondence (e.g. sedeti/sjediti, dete/dijete, odneti/odnijeti, predsednik/predsjednik, grešiti/griješiti) between this Ekavian Serbian-only source and earlier Ijekavian-leaning Croatian sources; recurs across every chunk of this book as a productive phonological pattern relevant to slang-synthesis mechanics analysis.

nodes.label: "Ekipa" Reading Strand (Colloquial-Register Narrative)
nodes.rationale: Recurring narrative thread following young Belgrade friends (Maja, Luka, Jelena, Filip, Sanja, Dado), used by the book across nearly every unit as its explicitly informal/colloquial register showcase, yielding the highest density of slang-adjacent items in this book.

nodes.label: super (colloquial exclamation)
nodes.rationale: English loanword used as a standalone colloquial exclamation ("Super! Slavimo!"), first Serbian-source-confirmed instance of this borrowing pattern in the project.

nodes.label: Belgrade Toponymy (Kalemegdan, Knez Mihajlova, Zeleni Venac, Dorćol, Zemun)
nodes.rationale: Belgrade-specific place names built into Units 4-5's city-tour dialogues and case-system examples; recurring geographic anchor for the book's narrative and a genuine cultural/geographic layer not present in the earlier sister textbook's arrival/hotel-focused Units 4-5.
nodes.norm_label: belgrade toponymy (kalemegdan, knez mihajlova, zeleni venac, dorcol, zemun)

nodes.label: живели/живјели Dialect Toast Contrast
nodes.rationale: Directly observed in-dialogue sociolinguistic contrast: Ekavian-speaking Belgrade hosts say живели! while Bosnian-heritage characters Dado and Sanja reply живјели! in the same toast scene, p.76 — primary evidence for Ekavian/Ijekavian variation distinct from descriptive sociolinguistic chapters elsewhere in the corpus.

nodes.label: Explicit Bosnian Ijekavian Dialect Flag (Sanja & Dado)
nodes.rationale: The source directly states that characters Sanja and Dado "speak the Bosnian Ijekavian dialect, using 'j' and 'ije' where Belgrade speech has 'e'" (p.101) — an explicit, source-authored dialect/register annotation of high value to this project's dialect-mapping goals.
nodes.norm_label: explicit bosnian ijekavian dialect flag (sanja & dado)

nodes.label: Cardinal Number System (0-5,000,000) and Agreement Rules
nodes.rationale: Full cardinal-number paradigm and the number-agreement rules (1 as adjective/indefinite article; 2/3/4 + genitive singular; 5+ + genitive plural with singular verb agreement) — introduced fresh in Unit 7, no precedent in the earlier sister textbook's corresponding units.
nodes.norm_label: cardinal number system (0-5,000,000) and agreement rules

nodes.label: escajg (source-marked colloquial register)
nodes.rationale: The source itself glosses escajg 'cutlery' explicitly as "a colloquial alternative to pribor za jelo" (p.107) — the clearest direct source-marked register annotation in this book's Units 7-9, high value for register tracking.

nodes.label: Serbian/Croatian Lexical Doublets (comparative dataset)
nodes.rationale: Cross-book comparison surfaces synonym pairs for the same referent (paradajz/rajčica, biber/papar, sirće/ocat, kajsija/marelica, sopstven/vlastit, niko/nitko, vazduh/zrak, bioskop/kino, fudbal/nogomet, konobar/kelner) — useful comparative Serbian/Croatian lexical data even though each concept individually is already covered.

nodes.label: Animal-Comparison Simile Template (X kao Y)
nodes.rationale: A productive fixed colloquial figurative-construction template (predicate-adjective + kao + animal): umoran kao pas, gladan kao vuk, tvrdoglav kao magarac, prljav kao svinja, glup kao vo, glupa kao guska (p.166) — flagged by the book itself as a pedagogical "work out what they mean" exercise, a strong candidate for slang-mechanics analysis.

nodes.label: Future Tense (hteti + infinitive) Full Paradigm
nodes.rationale: Fuller systematic tabulation than the sister textbook's prose-style treatment: separate Affirmative/Interrogative/Negative/Negative-interrogative columns for the short (ću) and long (hoću) hteti forms, plus the -ti-infinitive fusion rule (biću, spavaćeš, videćemo).

nodes.label: Kinship-Precision Vocabulary (strina/ujna/teča split)
nodes.rationale: Family-tree diagram distinguishes strina (paternal uncle's wife) from ujna (maternal uncle's wife) and notes tetka's husband is teča — a fuller kinship-precision system than the sister textbook's simpler "teta"-only coverage, genuinely deepening the corpus's kinship-terminology data.

nodes.label: Perfect Tense: Active Past Participle Formation
nodes.rationale: Core grammar point: Serbian compound perfect = present of biti + active past participle, with regular -ti/-sti endings and an irregular -ći/ići-compound set (stigao, mogao, rekao, išao, došao, ušao).
nodes.norm_label: perfect tense: active past participle formation

nodes.label: Sanja's Ijekavian Voice in "Ekipa" Unit 12
nodes.rationale: In the Unit 12 "Ekipa" installment (p.175), the otherwise-Ekavian narration is interrupted by character Sanja's visibly Ijekavian forms (svijeta, uvijek, mjeseci), used as a characterization device; the book's own vocabulary entry gives the pair uvijek/uvek explicitly side by side.

nodes.label: Comparative/Superlative Adjective & Adverb Formation
nodes.rationale: Units 14-15 comparative formation (-iji/-ija/-ije, consonant alternations k+j→č etc.), irregular comparatives (dobar→bolji), superlative naj- prefixation, and comparison constructions (od+gen., nego, sve+comparative, što+comparative) — substantively the same rule set already tabulated in the sister textbook, kept as a grammar concept node since the vocabulary/examples are independently new.

nodes.label: Serbian Music Genre Vocabulary (narodnjak, gusle, tambura, starogradska pesma)
nodes.rationale: Unit 13 dialogue covers a genuinely new domain (no precedent in the sister textbook): narodnjak (modern folk-pop), gusle (epic-song lute), tambura/tamburica (Vojvodina instrument), starogradska pesma (old urban song genre), and the trubački sabor u Guči festival explicitly tied to Kusturica's films' popularization of trubači abroad.
nodes.norm_label: serbian music genre vocabulary (narodnjak, gusle, tambura, starogradska pesma)

nodes.label: Novi Pazar / Sandžak Setting (Units 14-15)
nodes.rationale: Family road-trip narrative to Novi Pazar and Sopoćani Monastery; the book explicitly notes the town's predominantly Muslim/Bosniak population and Sandžak regional identity — genuine cultural/historical content absent from the Zagreb-set equivalent units of the sister textbook.

nodes.label: Sibling-Argument Colloquial Idiom Set
nodes.rationale: A packing-argument dialogue between sisters yields several fixed sharp-register idioms explicitly glossed by the source: gledati svoja posla "mind your own business", pustiti na miru "leave alone", ako ti je volja, manje-više, briga (sarcastic "Hvala na brizi").

nodes.label: гепек (colloquial car-boot term, < Ger. Gepäck)
nodes.rationale: Car-parts diagram (p.226) offers гепек as an unmarked colloquial alternative to пртљажник "boot/trunk", derived from German Gepäck — the single genuinely new lexical item vs. the sister textbook's equivalent car-vocabulary list, plus the source's unusual dual British/American glossing (bonnet/hood, boot/trunk).

nodes.label: ко/шта vs. tko/što Interrogative Variant
nodes.rationale: The interrogative-pronoun paradigm is structurally identical to the sister textbook's tko/što system but realized with the standard Serbian lexical variant ко/шта — a genuine, if unmarked-by-source, cross-book B/C/S contrast.

nodes.label: бака-сервис ("grandma service" colloquial coinage)
nodes.rationale: Dual-income-family joke term for informal grandparent-provided childcare; the exercise itself asks the learner to guess the meaning, confirming the book presents it as a colloquial coinage/idiom rather than standard vocabulary (pp.270-271).

nodes.label: Kotor/Budva/Cetinje/Lovćen Montenegrin Setting
nodes.rationale: First sustained Montenegrin-setting content in this project's Serbian corpus (Units 18-19), narrated in standard Ekavian Serbian despite the Montenegrin locale — the characters speak Belgrade-standard Ekavian rather than dialect Montenegrin.

nodes.label: плесати Regional Register Flag (Bosnia-Herzegovina/Croatia)
nodes.rationale: The source glosses плесати "to dance" explicitly as "(used in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia)" (p.262), yet the Kotor dialogue itself uses the verb — an explicit regional-register annotation applied to a word the narrative nonetheless deploys in standard Serbian dialogue.

nodes.label: посв(ј)етити се Ekavian/Ijekavian Isogloss Marking
nodes.rationale: The vocabulary box itself spells the headword посв(ј)етити се, registering the е/ије isogloss directly in the dictionary entry even though the book otherwise teaches pure Ekavian — the same axis documented at length in established/035_socioling_ch25_serbian_montenegro.md as the central Belgrade-standard vs. Montenegrin/Bosnian/Croatian dialect marker; the same word appears in dialogue as ijekavian "посвјетим" spoken by character Sanja.

nodes.label: Enclitic Placement and Information-Structure Word Order
nodes.rationale: Comprehensive treatment of the fixed enclitic ordering rule (li-verb-D,A/G-se-je), the first-stressed-element placement principle, and the broader Serbian information-structure word-order principle (less-informative-before-more-informative, stress building toward sentence end) — the book's own capstone syntax summary.
nodes.norm_label: enclitic placement and information-structure word order

nodes.label: Present/Past Gerund and Passive Participle System
nodes.rationale: Culminating Unit 20 grammar: present gerund (-ći from imperfective 3pl, e.g. budući), past gerund (-vši/-avši, rarely used except adjectivized bivši "former"), and passive past participle formation (-an/-en/-jen/-nut/-et) with derived verbal nouns in -је.

nodes.rationale: Monolingual Serbian-only end-of-book glossary (~1,337 rows across 4 parts, A-Ž) citing each entry's first-appearing unit number; unlike the sister Croatian-and-Serbian textbook's glossary, carries no B/C/S comparative tags since it is not a bridging dictionary.

nodes.label: Grammar Summary Chapter Redundancy Finding
nodes.rationale: This book's "Grammar summary" chapter (noun/adjective/pronoun declensions, verb types, mobile a, consonant changes, question formation, other tenses, collective numerals) was checked section-by-section against established/072 (the same author's earlier sister-book grammar summary) and found to be near-verbatim reused text, including the identical 'legenda→legendi' mobile-a example and the identical collective/distributive numeral paradigms already flagged by established/072 as its own genuinely-new find — confirming shared textual lineage across the author's two textbooks rather than independent content; net result was zero new vocabulary or grammar points extracted from this chunk.
